title: AI storytelling
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this lesson, students become author-illustrator teams working alongside AI. Each student (or pair) will invent a short story — a folktale, adventure, or funny anecdote — and use a text-based AI tool to help draft and polish the writing. They will then use an AI image generator to create illustrations that match their story's characters, settings, and mood. By the end of the session, each student will have a complete illustrated mini-story (3–6 pages) that they can present to the class, either as a simple printed booklet, a slideshow, or a digital document.

The goal is not just to produce a cute story, but to help students understand how AI can act as a creative collaborator — generating ideas, suggesting words, and turning descriptions into pictures — while the human remains the director, editor, and decision-maker. Students will practise clear instruction-writing (prompting), critical evaluation of AI output, and basic story structure (beginning, middle, end).

Tools & Resources

  • ChatGPT (free tier) — https://chat.openai.com — used for brainstorming plot ideas, drafting story text, and rewriting sentences. Free tier may show "usage limit reached" messages during busy periods; have a backup device or pair students up if this happens.
  • Microsoft Designer / Bing Image Creator — https://designer.microsoft.com — used to generate illustrations from text descriptions. Free accounts get a limited number of "boosted" fast generations per day (typically 15–25); after that, images generate more slowly. Requires a free Microsoft account and sign-in.
  • Canva (free tier) — https://canva.com — optional, for assembling the story text and AI images into a neat illustrated booklet or slideshow layout.
  • Google Docs or physical notebook — for drafting and organising story text before pasting into design tools.
  • Printed story-planning worksheet (one per student/pair) with boxes for: Character, Setting, Problem, Ending.

Connectivity note: Both AI tools require stable internet. If bandwidth is limited, consider having only the teacher or one device per group generate images, projecting results for shared discussion, while individual students focus on writing.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Warm-up discussion (5 min): Ask "What makes a story fun to read or a picture fun to look at?" List student answers on the board (characters, surprises, colour, humour).
  2. Story planning (10 min): Hand out the planning worksheet. Each student/pair fills in: Main Character (name + description), Setting (where/when), Problem (what goes wrong), and Ending (how it's solved). Example: Character — "Amina, a clever tortoise"; Setting — "a dry savanna during a drought"; Problem — "the animals can't find water"; Ending — "Amina remembers a hidden spring."
  3. Draft the story with AI (15 min): Students open ChatGPT and enter a prompt combining their planning notes, e.g.: "Write a short 5-paragraph children's story about a clever tortoise named Amina who helps thirsty animals find water during a drought in the savanna. Use simple language suitable for a young reader. End with a lesson about teamwork." Encourage students to read the output and ask AI to change things: "Make it funnier," or "Add a mischievous hyena character."
  4. Edit and personalise (10 min): Students copy the AI draft into a document and edit it in their own words — changing at least 3 sentences, adding a personal detail, or fixing anything that doesn't match their original plan. Emphasise: the AI text is a first draft, not the final answer.
  5. Break story into scenes (5 min): Students split their story into 3–5 short scenes/pages, one or two sentences each, to prepare for illustration.
  6. Generate illustrations (20 min): For each scene, students write an image prompt describing character, setting, action, and style, e.g.: "A friendly cartoon tortoise with a red bandana walking across a dry, cracked savanna under a hot sun, children's storybook illustration style, bright colours." Generate the image in Microsoft Designer/Bing Image Creator, review results, and regenerate with adjusted prompts if needed (e.g., "make the tortoise smaller," "add other animals in the background").
  7. Assemble the illustrated story (10 min): Paste text and matching images into Canva (or arrange printed pages) to create the final illustrated booklet or slideshow, in correct scene order.
  8. Share out (5–10 min): Volunteers read their story aloud or show their slides to the class.

Example Outputs

  • "Amina the Clever Tortoise": A 4-page story about a tortoise who solves a drought crisis using memory and teamwork, illustrated with warm savanna-toned cartoon images showing the tortoise, a worried elephant, and a hidden spring.
  • "The Boy Who Talked to Matatus": A humorous 5-scene story set in Nairobi about a boy who discovers his neighbourhood matatu can talk and give him life advice, illustrated in a bright, comic-style with colourful matatu artwork and city backgrounds.
  • "Nia and the Missing Stars": A short fantasy story where a girl uses a magic telescope to return stolen stars to the night sky, illustrated with a dreamy blue-and-purple palette, showing character growth from worried to confident across three scenes.

Facilitation Tips

  • Model the full process once on a projector before students start, showing both a text prompt and an image prompt, including what to do when the AI gives an unexpected or "wrong" result (simply rewrite the prompt — this is normal and expected, not a failure).
  • Keep an eye on pacing: writing tends to take longer than planned, illustration less so. Use a visible timer for each stage to keep the group moving together.
  • If AI-generated character appearance changes between images (e.g., the tortoise looks different in each scene), turn this into a teaching moment about AI's lack of memory between separate image requests — discuss how professional users solve this (character reference prompts, consistent descriptive keywords).
  • Some students may want to copy the entire AI story unedited — gently require the "3 sentence change" rule so every submission has a personal authorial touch.
  • Watch for inappropriate or odd image results (common with vague prompts); encourage specific, respectful language and review the image gallery on a shared screen if needed before students save their favourite image.
  • Pair weaker readers/writers with confident peers so both contribute to writing and prompting.

Discussion Questions

  • What did the AI do well when writing your story, and what did you have to change or fix yourself?
  • How is asking an AI for a picture different from asking a human artist to draw one for you?
  • Why did the AI sometimes draw your character differently in each image, even though you used the same name?
  • Who is the "author" of your final story — you, the AI, or both? Explain your answer.
  • If you used a vague prompt versus a very detailed one, how did the results differ? What does this teach us about giving instructions to AI?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a second illustrated scene to your story that wasn't in your original plan, and write one new sentence of dialogue for your main character.
  • Medium: Rewrite your story in a different genre (turn your adventure into a mystery, or your fairy tale into science fiction) using AI to help brainstorm the changes, then generate new matching illustrations.
  • Hard: Create a "choose your own adventure" version of your story with at least two branching points, where the reader picks what the character does next — requiring multiple AI-generated text branches and matching illustrations for each path.
